data.title: Persistence via Existing-Service Modification
data.summary: Rather than creating a new service, the sample reconfigures an existing one's binary path or startup parameters so the legitimate service launches the malicious payload instead of its original executable.
data.description:
This avoids the detection attention a brand-new, unfamiliar service name attracts: the
service still appears in listings under its original, familiar name, and only its
configured binary path has changed. Because modifying a service's configuration typically
requires administrative privilege, successful use of this technique is itself evidence
that privilege escalation has already occurred on the host.
data.recommendation:
* Diff service configurations (binary path, startup parameters) against a known-good baseline rather than relying on service name or display name alone, which will look unchanged.
* Treat confirmed use of this technique as proof administrative privilege was already obtained, and investigate how that occurred as a separate finding.
* Restore the original service binary path and restart the service rather than merely stopping the malicious process, which the service will otherwise relaunch.
data.short_recommendation: Diff service binary paths against a known-good baseline; the service name will look unchanged even when hijacked.

mitre_techniques.procedure: Used the service control manager to change an existing, legitimate service's binary path to point at the malicious payload, then restarted the service.

mbc_techniques.implementation: Reconfigured an existing service's binary path to launch the payload under its established, trusted service identity.
